# Calling StrongHold from Lovable

**StrongHold** is a sovereign, memory-centric AI-agent harness served as an API ("Harness as a Service") — same capabilities as a cloud AI-agent service, but it runs entirely on the owner's own hardware (two DGX Sparks), data stays local.

**Base URL:** `https://spark-47d8.tail333a1d.ts.net/agentmem/v1`
**Auth:** `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>` on every request except `GET /health`.
**CORS:** enabled — works from any Lovable preview/custom domain.
**Streaming:** `POST /agents/{id}/chat` returns SSE when `Accept: text/event-stream`.
Use `fetch` + a stream reader for streaming — **not** `EventSource` (it can't send the `Authorization` header).
**Rate limits:** per-tenant token bucket (heavy ops cost more). Be a good client — handle `429` with `Retry-After` (see [Rate limits](#rate-limits)).

## Token

For getting started, one shared long-lived HS256 test token (sub `lovable-user`):

```
<PASTE_TEST_TOKEN>
```

> ⚠️ This single token is visible in the browser bundle and maps everyone to ONE user. Fine for a prototype. For real per-user memory, use Supabase auth (see [bottom](#production-auth-per-user-via-supabase--already-wired-zero-config)) so each signed-in user gets their own isolated memory.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Body | Returns |
|--------|------|------|---------|
| GET  | `/health` | — | `{status, baseVectors, internal}` (no auth) |
| GET  | `/agents` | — | `Agent[]` (caller's agents) |
| POST | `/agents` | `{agentType, label?}` | `Agent` |
| GET  | `/agents/{id}` | — | `Agent` |
| DELETE | `/agents/{id}` | — | `{agentId, promoted:{ingested,deleted}, gatedOut}` (graduate-on-terminate) |
| POST | `/agents/{id}/memories` | `{text: string \| string[]}` | `{ids, count}` (durable before it returns 200/201) |
| POST | `/agents/{id}/recall` | `{query, k?}` | `MemoryHit[]` (base ∪ this agent's private; child wins) |
| POST | `/agents/{id}/chat` | `{prompt, tier?, recallK?}` | `{text, provider, model, usedMemories, usage}` or SSE |
| POST | `/agents/{id}/act` | `{prompt, tier?, profile?, tools?, maxSteps?, recallK?}` | `{text, steps[], usedMemories, provider, model, usage}` — **agentic loop** |
| POST | `/agents/{id}/fanout` | `{tasks[], tier?, profile?, tools?, agentType?, maxStepsPer?}` | aggregated sub-agent results (incl. `usage`) |
| POST | `/sandbox/run` | `{language, code, timeoutMs?}` | `{stdout, stderr, exitCode, timedOut, durationMs}` |
| POST | `/memory/search` | `{query, k?}` | `MemoryHit[]` (caller's shared base) |

`Agent = {agentId, agentType, label, status, createdAt}`
`MemoryHit = {id, text, distance /* lower = closer */, source /* 'base' or agentId */}`
`Usage = {input, output, total}` — token counts for the request, so you can show cost/usage per call. On `chat` it's the single model call; on `act` / `fanout` it's **summed across the whole agentic loop / all sub-agents**.

### `/act` — the agentic loop

The model recalls relevant memories, injects them, then calls tools (run code in the sandbox, recall/remember memory, and any permitted external tools), feeds results back, and returns a concise final answer. `steps[]` is the trace (`{tool, args, result}`).
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
### `/fanout` — sub-agent fan-out

Up to 8 ephemeral workers run `tasks[]` in parallel, results are aggregated, then the workers are dismissed (no graduation). `tasks` can be plain strings or per-task objects `{prompt, tools?, profile?}`, so each worker can get its own toolset. Top-level `tier` / `profile` / `tools` / `agentType` / `maxStepsPer` apply as defaults.

### `/sandbox/run` — sovereign code sandbox

Hardened ephemeral Docker container: `--network none`, all caps dropped, read-only rootfs, non-root, `/tmp` tmpfs noexec, memory/CPU/pids/time limited. Languages: `python`, `node`, `bash`. No network from inside.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
## Picking quality vs. speed — the `tier` knob (optional)

You never name a model. Add an optional `tier` to `chat` / `act` / `fanout`; omit it and you get smart defaults. Every response reports the `provider` (`local` / `cloud` / `openrouter`) and `model` that actually answered.

| `tier` | What you get |
|---|---|
| `"fast"` / `"balanced"` | Local model — free, private, on your hardware. |
| *(omitted)* / `"auto"` | **Local first**, transparently falls over to cloud Claude, then OpenRouter. Good default. |
| `"max"` | **Best reasoning** — cloud Claude (Opus), falls back to OpenRouter then local. |
| `"openrouter"` | Route to OpenRouter (GPT/Gemini/Llama/…), local fallback. |

Local inference is load-balanced across **both DGX Sparks** (two GPUs = true parallelism), so fan-out and concurrent chats don't all pile onto one GPU. If a provider's key isn't set, *every* tier transparently skips it — nothing breaks, you just don't get that option. Example: `AgentMemory.chat(id, prompt, { tier: "max" })`.

**Pick a specific model (power users):** instead of (or alongside) `tier`, pass an explicit `model`. An **explicit `model` wins routing** over the tier's defaults:
- A **bare model id** (e.g. `{ model: "deepseek-r1:32b" }`) routes to the local Ollama pool — any model loaded on the cluster is reachable by name, not just the default.
- A **`prefix/model` slug** routes by its prefix: if the prefix is a configured OpenAI-compatible backend name it goes there (`{ model: "webui/llama3.1:70b" }`), otherwise it's treated as an OpenRouter vendor slug (`{ model: "google/gemini-2.0-flash" }`). Which backends exist is a server-side config detail.

Most callers should just use `tier` and never name a model.

`GET /health`'s `router.{cloud,openrouter}` flip from `false` to the model name when those keys are configured. Data leaves your hardware only for cloud/OpenRouter requests — `fast`/`balanced` always stay local.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
## Choosing tools per task — the `profile` / `tools` knob (act + fanout)

By default an agent can use **all** tools. To scope what the model is allowed to touch on a given `/act` (or `/fanout`) call, pass either a named `profile` **or** an explicit `tools` allowlist. Scoping is enforced two ways: the filtered set is what's *offered* to the model, and any call to a non-permitted tool is rejected at dispatch with "not permitted".

Built-in profiles:

| `profile` | Tools the agent can use |
|---|---|
| `all` | Everything (the default if you pass nothing) |
| `memory` | Recall / remember only |
| `code` | Run code in the sandbox |
| `files` | LucidLink filespace tools (`lucidlink__*`) |
| `research` | Files + memory + code for read/search-heavy work |
| `lucid-readonly` | Read-only LucidLink access |

```ts
// Let the agent read & search the team's LucidLink files while answering:
AgentMemory.act(id, "Summarize the latest project brief in our filespace", { profile: "research" });

// Or an explicit allowlist (names, "server__tool", or "*" wildcard):
AgentMemory.act(id, "...", { tools: ["recall_memory", "lucidlink__read_file", "lucidlink__grep_files"] });
```

### LucidLink filespace tools

With the `files` / `research` / `lucid-readonly` profile, the agent gains **read-only** access to the team's LucidLink filespaces: `list_filespaces`, `link_filespace`, `current_filespace`, `whoami`, `read_file`, `list_files`, `find_files`, `grep_files`, `read_lines`. So an `/act` agent can locate, search, and read the team's actual files to ground its answer — it cannot write or delete. (Owner-scoped v1: one service-account view shared across tenants.)
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
## Rate limits

Each tenant gets a token bucket (burst capacity ~30, refill ~1/sec). Heavy ops — `act`, `fanout`, `chat`, `sandbox/run` — cost ~5 each, and there's a global cap on simultaneous heavy jobs. When you exceed it the API returns **`429`** with a **`Retry-After`** header (seconds). Be a good client: back off and retry after that delay rather than hammering. The `api()` helper above surfaces the `Retry-After` so you can schedule the retry. Also note request bodies over ~1 MB return `413`.

## Prompt to paste into Lovable

> Build a chat UI backed by my StrongHold API at
> `https://spark-47d8.tail333a1d.ts.net/agentmem/v1`. Use the client in
> `src/lib/agentMemory.ts` (already added). On first load, call `spawn("assistant")`
> and keep the returned `agentId`. Send chat with `AgentMemory.chatStream(agentId, prompt, onDelta)`
> and render tokens as they arrive. Add a "remember this" button that calls
> `remember(agentId, text)`, and a search box that calls `searchBase(query)`. Add a
> "research" action that calls `act(agentId, q, { profile: "research" })` so the agent
> can read our LucidLink files. Auth is a Bearer token already wired in `getToken()`.
> If a call throws a "rate limited" error, show a toast and retry after the delay.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
## Production auth (per-user, via Supabase) — ALREADY WIRED, zero config

The backend already verifies real Supabase user tokens for **any** of your projects —
past, present, or future — with no per-project setup. It detects the token's signing
algorithm and, for Supabase asymmetric tokens (RS256/ES256/PS256, what every current
project uses), fetches the JWKS of the **token's own issuer**
(`https://<ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1`), verifies the signature, and scopes memory to
`"<projectRef>:<userId>"` — so the same user UUID in two different projects is two
isolated tenants. JWKS is cached and refetched on key rotation (and a briefly
unreachable IdP serves the last-good key rather than failing every login). The HS256
prototype token keeps working alongside.

In Lovable, just point `getToken()` at the Supabase session (make `api()` await it):

```ts
const getToken = async () =>
  (await supabase.auth.getSession()).data.session?.access_token ?? "";
```

That's it — no backend change needed when you add new Supabase projects.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

text:
### Locked to your projects (active)

The API is restricted to an allowlist of Supabase project refs (`SUPABASE_ALLOWED_REFS`
in `backend/.env`). It **fails closed**: with no allowlist set, asymmetric tokens are
rejected unless `SUPABASE_ALLOW_ANY=1`. Tokens from any non-allowed project are rejected
with `project not allowed`.

**To onboard another Lovable project** (new or existing): find its ref — the `<ref>` in
`https://<ref>.supabase.co` (Lovable → Supabase integration, or Supabase dashboard →
Project Settings → API → Project URL) — append it to the comma-separated list in
`backend/.env`, then:

```
cd /home/markt/agenticow-ruflo-memory/backend && docker compose up -d
```

No code change, no rebuild — the new project's signed-in users authenticate immediately,
each isolated as `"<ref>:<userId>"`. To **remove** a project, delete its ref and redeploy.

Legacy HS256-only projects: set `JWT_SECRET` to that project's JWT Secret (this also
disables the shared prototype test token). Rotate `JWT_SECRET` to a fresh random value to
kill the prototype token.
title: Calling StrongHold from Lovable

# ADR-0001: Two-tier topology — internal harness + public backend

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

StrongHold exposes an LLM harness (memory, agentic loop, sandbox, MCP tools) to a
customer-facing app (Lovable) over the public internet via a Tailscale Funnel. The
harness holds everything sensitive: model API keys, the memory corpus, MCP server
credentials, and the ability to spawn/delete any agent and run a code sandbox. A
single process facing the internet would put all of that one bug away from
compromise, and would couple the public contract to the internal implementation.

## Decision

Split into two processes:

- **Tier 1 — internal harness** (`service/server.js`, Fastify, `:8770`). Holds all
  capability and all secrets. Authenticated by a single `X-API-Key`. Addresses
  agents by `agentId`; knows nothing about end users. Bound to localhost + the
  Docker bridge.
- **Tier 2 — public backend** (`backend/server.js`, zero-dependency
  `node:http` + `node:crypto`, `:8771`). The only internet-facing edge. Verifies
  the Bearer JWT, derives the tenant from the token (never the body), enforces
  per-tenant ownership, applies CORS / rate limits / body caps, and proxies to
  Tier 1. Holds **no** model keys and **no** memory — only a tenant→agent
  ownership map.

The backend is co-located on spark with the internal service (reachable via
`host.docker.internal`), not on a separate host — simpler, and relocatable by
repointing `INTERNAL_URL`.
title: ADR-0001: Two-tier topology — internal harness + public backend

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** the internet-facing surface is tiny and dependency-free (small
  image, nothing to `npm audit`); secrets never live at the edge; the public API
  contract (`openapi.yaml`) is decoupled from the internal implementation; abuse
  controls live at the edge where the tenant identity is known.
- **Negative:** an extra network hop and a second process to operate; the
  ownership map (`owners.json`) is a small stateful component the backend must
  persist and protect.
- **Neutral:** the internal service's strong `X-API-Key` becomes the trust anchor
  between tiers — see ADR-0004 for why the internal service is also deprivileged.

## Alternatives considered

- **Single process.** Rejected: couples public contract to internals and exposes
  all secrets/capability at the internet edge.
- **Backend on a separate host (ai-factory-mini).** Deferred: more moving parts;
  co-location is simpler and the split is what matters for the security boundary.
title: ADR-0001: Two-tier topology — internal harness + public backend

# ADR-0002: Append-only durable log is the source of truth

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

Memory is built on **agenticow** (copy-on-write vector branching — "Git for agent
memory"). Its persistence (`*.rvf` + manifest) saves **vectors but not the text
payloads**. So a naive reload survived the vector *count* but returned hits with
`undefined` text — memory content did not actually survive a restart, and the
service is reboot-safe (it *will* restart). The per-user base-agent id cached in
the backend also didn't survive an internal restart, causing `agent not found`.

## Decision

Make a tiny **append-only log of `{id, text, scope, vector?}`** the *source of
truth* (`src/durable-store.js`, `<BASE_PATH>.durable.json`). On every boot the
service **wipes the agenticow vector files and rebuilds the in-RAM index from the
log** (`bridge.rehydrate()`), re-embedding only entries that lack a persisted
vector. `scope` is `base`, a per-agent id, or (later) `tbase:<tenant>`.

Supporting rules:
- `remember()` **flushes the log before acknowledging** — a 201 never lies about
  durability.
- The persisted embedding vector (base64 `Float32`) lives alongside the text, so
  rehydrate is ~O(load), not O(re-embed corpus).
- A corrupt log is **backed up and the service refuses to start** rather than
  silently blanking memory.
title: ADR-0002: Append-only durable log is the source of truth

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** memory (with text) survives restarts/reboots deterministically;
  embeddings are local + deterministic so a rebuild is exact; the log is a simple,
  inspectable, greppable file; it doubles as the unit of cross-machine sync
  (ADR-0008) and the substrate for per-tenant grouping (ADR-0009).
- **Negative:** writes happen twice (agenticow index + log); the full log is read
  into memory at boot (fine at current corpus size, revisit at very large scale);
  the agenticow manifest path is now effectively vestigial.
- **Neutral:** rehydrate is the one place that must understand every scope kind,
  so scope semantics (graduation, tenancy) are centralized there.

## Alternatives considered

- **Trust the agenticow manifest.** Rejected: it loses text — the actual content.
- **A real embedded DB (SQLite/LMDB).** Overkill for the corpus size and would add
  a dependency to a service that prizes a tiny surface; the append-only JSON log is
  enough and trivially portable.
title: ADR-0002: Append-only durable log is the source of truth

# ADR-0003: Dual-mode JWT auth — HS256 + multi-project Supabase JWKS

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

The public backend must authenticate users from a customer-facing app and derive a
stable, isolated tenant key per user. The app stack is Supabase (which issues
**asymmetric** RS/ES/PS JWTs per project, rotating keys via JWKS), but we also need
a simple long-lived token for prototypes, local tooling, and the MCP wrapper. We
did not want per-project configuration or a shared secret shipped in browser
bundles to be the only option.

## Decision

Verify the Bearer JWT with the algorithm **auto-detected from the token header**:

- **Asymmetric (RS/ES/PS)** — verify against the **JWKS of the token's OWN issuer**
  (`https://<ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1`, validated by `SUPABASE_ISS_REGEX`). Any of
  the owner's Supabase projects — past or future — works with zero config. Tenant
  key = `"<ref>:<sub>"`, so the same user UUID in two projects is two isolated
  tenants. JWKS is cached per-issuer (1h) and refetched on an unknown `kid`; if the
  IdP is briefly unreachable the last-good key is served rather than failing every
  login.
- **HS256** — verify against `JWT_SECRET`; tenant `"hs:<sub>"`. For the prototype
  token, single-secret/legacy projects, and the MCP wrapper.

**Fail closed:** with no `SUPABASE_ALLOWED_REFS` allowlist, asymmetric tokens are
**rejected** unless `SUPABASE_ALLOW_ANY=1` is explicitly set (otherwise anyone with
any Supabase account could spawn agents and burn the model budget). The backend
also refuses to boot on a weak/default `JWT_SECRET` or `INTERNAL_API_KEY`.

`userId` always comes from the `sub` claim — **never** the request body.
title: ADR-0003: Dual-mode JWT auth — HS256 + multi-project Supabase JWKS

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** zero-config onboarding of any of the owner's Supabase projects;
  cross-project tenant isolation for free; key rotation handled via JWKS; a simple
  escape hatch (HS256) for non-Supabase clients; open-registration cost-abuse is
  closed by default.
- **Negative:** two code paths to maintain; the HS256 prototype token, if leaked,
  maps everyone to one tenant until `JWT_SECRET` is rotated (tracked as a residual
  risk); JWKS adds an outbound dependency on the IdP (mitigated by the stale-cache
  fallback).
- **Neutral:** the tenant key shape (`<ref>:<sub>` / `hs:<sub>`) is the seam every
  downstream isolation layer keys off (ADR-0009).

## Alternatives considered

- **Single shared HS256 secret only.** Rejected: doesn't fit Supabase's asymmetric,
  rotating, per-project keys; forces secret distribution.
- **Static per-project JWKS config.** Rejected: every new project needs a config
  change; deriving JWKS from the token's own issuer + an allowlist is zero-touch.
title: ADR-0003: Dual-mode JWT auth — HS256 + multi-project Supabase JWKS

# ADR-0004: Run the harness as an unprivileged user on its own rootless Docker

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

The harness runs model-generated code in Docker containers (ADR-0006). Initially
the internal service ran as `markt`, who is in the `docker` group. Membership of
the `docker` group is effectively **host root** (the Docker socket can mount the
host filesystem). So an RCE in the harness process *itself* — not the sandbox, the
host service — would own the box. That is too much blast radius for an
internet-reachable service.

## Decision

Run the internal service as a dedicated unprivileged user **`stronghold`** (uid
1001, **not** in the `docker` group, locked password, own home, `subuid`/`subgid`
range) talking to its **own rootless Docker daemon**
(`systemctl --user docker.service`, socket `unix:///run/user/1001/docker.sock`).
Sandbox container UID 0 maps to `stronghold`'s subuid range — powerless on the
host. The app stays in place at `/home/markt/agenticow-ruflo-memory`; `stronghold`
gets surgical **POSIX ACLs** (traverse `/home/markt`, `rwX` on the app dir and the
ruflo registry/agent-store, read on the bridge's SSH key) rather than relocating
the app. `markt` keeps `docker`-group membership for the rootful fleet
(ruvector, the backend container, etc.).
title: ADR-0004: Run the harness as an unprivileged user on its own rootless Docker

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** a harness RCE no longer implies host root — it lands as an
  unprivileged user with no rootful socket; container escape maps to an
  unprivileged subuid, not host root (verified: container-root cannot write a
  markt-owned file and appears as `nobody`); the rootful daemon never runs sandbox
  containers.
- **Negative:** operational complexity (rootless dockerd, `subuid`/`subgid`,
  `linger`, ACLs); some sharp edges hit during migration (MCP children needed
  explicit `HOME`/known_hosts ACLs; the npx cache under the new HOME had to be
  re-warmed). Never ACL a *private key* — it bumps the group bits and `ssh` then
  refuses it.
- **Neutral:** the internal `X-API-Key` (ADR-0001) and this deprivileging together
  define the Tier-1 trust boundary.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep running as a docker-group user.** Rejected: harness RCE = host root.
- **Rootful Docker with `--userns-remap`.** Partial; rootless is a stronger, more
  self-contained boundary and keeps the harness off the rootful socket entirely.
- **gVisor / Kata / Firecracker.** Heavier; the rootless + hardened-container combo
  (ADR-0006) is sufficient for the current threat model and far simpler to operate.
title: ADR-0004: Run the harness as an unprivileged user on its own rootless Docker

# ADR-0005: Provider-agnostic model router with a single `tier` knob

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

The whole thesis of StrongHold is a **metaharness**: the model is a swappable
component, not the fixed center of a vendor's harness. Callers should ask for a
*quality/cost tier*, not name a model — and the system should fail over across
providers (local GPU, Claude, OpenRouter) without callers knowing. But the
providers disagree on wire format (OpenAI-style `tool_calls` vs Anthropic
`tool_use`/`tool_result`, system-message handling), and a single local 32B GPU
serializes concurrent work.

## Decision

A router (`service/router.js`) exposes one **`tier`** knob on chat/act/fanout;
callers never name a model (unless they pass an explicit `model`):

- `fast`/`balanced` → local only; `auto` → local→cloud failover; `max` →
  cloud→local. Providers: **local** = Ollama pool (`service/ollama.js`), **cloud**
  = Claude via `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, plus **OpenRouter** (`service/openrouter.js`,
  OpenAI-compatible) as failover / explicit tier. Each provider is enabled only
  when its key is present, else that tier silently runs local (graceful).
- The router translates messages and tools **OpenAI ↔ Anthropic** so the agentic
  loop is provider-independent (merges consecutive tool results into one user
  turn, drops empty assistant turns — Anthropic rejects those).
- The local backend is a **health-aware pool** (`OLLAMA_URLS`): each GPU host gets
  a one-job semaphore for true N-way parallelism, a host is healthy only if
  reachable *and* holding the model, and a failed call fails over to a sibling
  host before the router escalates to cloud. Every model call has an AbortSignal
  timeout so a hung host triggers failover instead of hanging.
title: ADR-0005: Provider-agnostic model router with a single `tier` knob

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** the metaharness promise is real — swap/add models by editing
  `OLLAMA_URLS` or a key, no caller changes; graceful degradation when a provider
  is down or unkeyed; genuine local parallelism across two DGX Sparks.
- **Negative:** message/tool translation is fiddly and a real source of edge cases
  (each provider's quirks must be handled); a tier's behavior depends on which keys
  are configured, which can surprise.
- **Neutral:** tool-call recovery from *text* content (some local models emit tool
  calls as prose) lives next to the router in the act loop (ADR-0007).

## Alternatives considered

- **Caller names the model.** Rejected: leaks provider choice into every client and
  defeats the swappable-model thesis.
- **One provider.** Rejected: no failover, no cost/quality control, vendor lock-in.
- **An off-the-shelf gateway (LiteLLM etc.).** Rejected for now: another dependency
  and process; the translation we need is small and the router stays in-process.
title: ADR-0005: Provider-agnostic model router with a single `tier` knob

text:
## Update 2026-06-30 (commit 68342fe)

The router widens from "one local model + cloud" to **any model on the cluster +
any OpenAI-compatible engine**, all selectable by config — without breaking the
`tier`-only contract. Three additions, all backward compatible (empty config =
exactly prior behavior):

- **Model-aware Ollama pool.** Each request now routes to a pool host that actually
  *has* the requested model, and the health gate no longer requires the single
  default model — a host is healthy if reachable and holding *some* model. Extra
  models already loaded on the cluster Ollamas (`deepseek-r1:32b`, `qwen2.5:32b`,
  `llama3.1:70b`) are reachable and metered by name with **zero config**. Bare
  model names still go to the Ollama pool and are never shadowed by a compat backend.
- **Generic OpenAI-compatible provider** (`service/openai-compat.js`): a config
  registry of named backends `{ name, url, apiKey?, models? }` for any
  OpenAI-compatible server (vLLM, llama.cpp `--server`, TGI, Open WebUI, LM Studio).
  Config source, first found: env `LLM_BACKENDS` (inline JSON) → env
  `LLM_BACKENDS_CONFIG` (path) → `./llm-backends.json`. Target a backend with an
  explicit `"<name>/<model>"` slug (e.g. `"webui/llama3.1:70b"`); usage is metered
  under provider label `compat:<name>`. Real config files are gitignored (keys +
  private URLs); only `*.example` templates are committed. Optional
  `COMPAT_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 120000) bounds compat calls.
- **Tier→model aliases (`TIER_MODELS`).** Two selection modes now coexist: (a) an
  explicit model slug **wins** routing — route by what the model *is*, not the
  tier's default provider order; (b) optional tier→model aliases (env `TIER_MODELS`
  inline JSON → env `TIER_MODELS_CONFIG` → `./tier-models.json`), e.g.
  `{"reason":"deepseek-r1:32b","big":"webui/llama3.1:70b"}`, so a bare `tier`
  resolves to a specific cluster model. `providersFor` only routes by model when one
  is given, else the tier order is unchanged.

`routerInfo` (`/healthz.router`) now also reports `compat` (array of backend names,
or `false`) and `tierModels`. The Docker public backend (:8771) needs no rebuild —
it proxies chat/act/fanout verbatim. Activation: `cp llm-backends.json.example
llm-backends.json` (fill URL + key), optionally `cp tier-models.json.example
tier-models.json`, then restart the internal service; extra Ollama models need none.

- **Consequence:** the metaharness promise widens — more/larger/specialized local
  models and any OpenAI-compatible engine are swappable purely by config, no code
  change, and (with ADR-0011 metering) every backend's token spend is visible.
title: ADR-0005: Provider-agnostic model router with a single `tier` knob

# ADR-0006: Sovereign sandbox — hardened ephemeral containers for model code

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

To match (and exceed) a hosted "Harness as a Service," the agentic loop needs to
*run* code the model writes — compute, verify, transform — not just talk about it.
That means executing arbitrary, model-generated code automatically, on our own
hardware, reachable (behind auth) from the public edge. This is sovereign RCE by
design; the entire question is containment.

## Decision

`service/sandbox.js` runs each `run_code` / `/sandbox/run` request in an
**ephemeral, hardened Docker container**, then removes it:

`--network none --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --read-only
--tmpfs /tmp (noexec) --user 1000:1000 --memory 512m --cpus 1 --pids-limit 128
--rm`, with a timeout that `docker kill`s the container.

Languages: python, node, bash. Gated by `SANDBOX_ENABLED` (a kill switch). A global
container semaphore (`SANDBOX_MAX_CONCURRENCY`) prevents fan-out from exhausting
host RAM. The daemon it runs on is `stronghold`'s **rootless** Docker (ADR-0004),
so even a container escape lands on an unprivileged subuid, not host root.

## Consequences

- **Positive:** the harness can actually do work (verified: it wrote and ran code
  to compute results inside the act loop); no network, no caps, non-root, read-only
  FS, `noexec` /tmp, and resource caps make the escape surface small; layered with
  rootless Docker for defense in depth; one switch disables it entirely.
- **Negative:** it is still arbitrary code execution — the residual risk is the
  container-escape surface itself, accepted and mitigated rather than eliminated;
  per-run container creation has latency (a warm pool was rejected — it would break
  per-run isolation).
- **Neutral:** sandbox concurrency shares the same abuse-control philosophy as the
  rate limiter (ADR-0001's edge controls).
title: ADR-0006: Sovereign sandbox — hardened ephemeral containers for model code

text:
## Alternatives considered

- **No sandbox (describe-only).** Rejected: that's the gap a real harness fills.
- **MicroVMs (Firecracker/Kata) or gVisor.** Stronger isolation but much heavier to
  operate; revisit if the threat model hardens. The current flags + rootless daemon
  are sufficient for internal use and a controlled pilot.
- **Warm container pool for latency.** Rejected: breaks the per-run isolation that
  is the whole point.
title: ADR-0006: Sovereign sandbox — hardened ephemeral containers for model code

# ADR-0007: External tools via an MCP hub + per-task tool profiles

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-29

## Context

The harness should reach external capability (ruflo's coordination tools,
read/write access to LucidLink filespaces) without bespoke integrations, and it
should be able to *scope* which tools a given task may use — both for safety
(don't offer write tools to a doc-summarizing task) and for steering the model.
External MCP servers are separate processes that can crash or hang.

## Decision

A generic MCP client + **`McpHub`** (`service/mcp-client.js`) speaks JSON-RPC over
stdio to multiple servers, namespacing tools `<server>__<tool>` with a per-server
`include`/`exclude` allowlist. Configured via `mcp-servers.json`. Dead children are
**auto-respawned with exponential backoff**; the act loop reads tools **live** via
`mcpHub.toolDefs()` (only *ready* servers), so a crashed-then-respawned server drops
out of and back into the toolset automatically. MCP children get a **minimal env
allowlist** (no secrets leak to third-party packages).

**Per-task tool selection** (`service/server.js`): `/act` and `/fanout` accept a
one-word `profile` (named bundle in `tool-profiles.json`) **or** an explicit
`tools` allowlist (names, `server__tool`, or `*`). Selection filters the tools
*offered* to the model **and** is enforced at *dispatch* (`allowedNames`) — a tool
call the task isn't permitted returns "not permitted" even if the model conjures
it. No selection = all tools (back-compat).
title: ADR-0007: External tools via an MCP hub + per-task tool profiles

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** new external capability is a config entry, not code; the harness
  survives flaky/crashing MCP servers; tasks run with least privilege and
  defense-in-depth (offered *and* enforced); secrets don't leak into third-party
  MCP processes; profiles are the seam for a future per-tenant saved-tool UX.
- **Negative:** stdio MCP processes are operational weight (respawn, env, known
  hosts); namespacing and the truncation/quirks of each server must be handled;
  the per-task knob is per-request today, not yet per-tenant-persisted.
- **Neutral:** the same selection mechanism gates the confined LucidLink write
  bridge (ADR-0008) — e.g. the `lucid-rw` profile.

## Alternatives considered

- **Hard-coded integrations per tool.** Rejected: doesn't scale, no uniform
  lifecycle/allowlisting.
- **Offer all tools always.** Rejected: unsafe (write/destructive tools exposed to
  every task) and worse for steering the model.
title: ADR-0007: External tools via an MCP hub + per-task tool profiles

text:
# ADR-0008: LucidLink as canonical cross-agent memory — one common namespace

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-30

## Context

The per-agent COW memory (ADR-0002) is a *semantic index* local to one box. The
product promise is **no memory handoffs**: agents on different machines/sites, and
the human's own Claude markdown memory, should share one canonical, durable,
lock-coordinated store. LucidLink (the filespace product — globally consistent,
E2E-encrypted, Raft-locked) is that store. Constraints: spark is `aarch64` and
`lucidlink` ships no ARM-Linux wheel (can't mount on spark); an agent with write
access must not be able to roam the whole account or destroy data.

## Decision

Access LucidLink over the MCP bridge (ADR-0007), with **two** bridges:

- **`lucidlink`** — broad **read-only** (core toolset, 9 tools) for doc processing.
- **`lucidlink-rw`** — full data plane (write + Raft locking tools) but **confined
  to a single filespace** (`agenticow`) = the common namespace `/stronghold-mem`.

The confinement boundary is **the filespace, enforced on the Mac**: a dedicated
key's `authorized_keys` pins a forced command
`LUCIDLINK_FILESPACE=agenticow … uvx lucidlink-mcp` (overrides anything spark
sends), and the spark-side `include` allowlist drops every destructive op
(no delete/move/rename) and omits `link_filespace`. There is no path-jail in
`lucidlink-mcp`, so the filespace is the only hard write boundary. spark can't
mount LucidLink, so a sync (`service/mem-sync.mjs`, `flock`-guarded systemd timer)
**streams** COW memory + Claude markdown memory into the namespace through the same
confined bridge. `write_file(exclusive=true)` uses Raft global locking for safe
concurrent multi-agent writes.
title: ADR-0008: LucidLink as canonical cross-agent memory — one common namespace

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** one canonical, cross-machine, encrypted, lock-coordinated memory
  namespace — the headline "no handoffs" feature; a 1:1 proof-point of LucidLink's
  own agentic-scaling positioning; the write boundary is enforced *server-side* on
  the Mac, not trusted from the client.
- **Negative:** depends on ai-factory-mini being awake (it sleeps after macOS
  updates); MCP rate limits throttle bulk sync (handled with backoff + pacing);
  `write_file` rejects some `.json` as a string, so non-`.md` is sent base64;
  `stronghold` reuses access via ACLs/keys that must be maintained.
- **Neutral:** the namespace is **owner-scoped** in v0.1 — the per-tenant layout
  on top of it is ADR-0009; per-tenant *filespaces* are the multi-org upgrade.

## Alternatives considered

- **Mount LucidLink on spark.** Impossible: no ARM-Linux wheel.
- **Direct S3 to the managed filespace.** Not available for the LucidLink-managed
  fs; the MCP bridge is the supported path.
- **One broad read/write bridge.** Rejected: an agent could leave the namespace or
  delete data — hence the second, confined, destructive-op-free bridge.
title: ADR-0008: LucidLink as canonical cross-agent memory — one common namespace

text:
# ADR-0009: Per-tenant memory isolation via tenant-scoped graduation + replay

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-30

## Context

Per-agent memories were already private, and agent *ownership* was enforced at the
backend (cross-tenant access → 404). But **graduation leaked across tenants**:
deleting an agent promoted its vetted learnings (`promoteTo`) into the *one* shared
agenticow base, and **every** agent of **every** tenant forks off that single base
— so tenant B recalled tenant A's graduated content (and `/memory/search`, routed
through a per-user base agent that also forked the shared base, did too). This was
the documented `v0.1` residual risk #2 and a hard blocker for multi-org use.

Structural fact: agenticow's `fork(base)` makes one base the parent of all
branches. Giving tenant A's agents a different base than tenant B's means either
**separate `AgenticMemory` instances per tenant** (per-tenant hubs) or **not using
the shared base for tenant-private graduation at all**.
title: ADR-0009: Per-tenant memory isolation via tenant-scoped graduation + replay

text:
## Decision

Keep **one** agenticow instance; make **graduation and recall tenant-scoped**:

1. Tag each agent with its `tenant` (the backend's JWT-derived key, ADR-0003) on
   spawn; persist it in the ruflo agent-store record.
2. `graduate()` re-scopes a tenant agent's learnings into a **per-tenant durable
   scope `tbase:<tenant>`** (`DurableStore.graduate(scope, toScope)`) and **does
   not** `promoteTo` the shared agenticow base.
3. Every one of a tenant's agents **inherits `tbase:<tenant>`** into its branch at
   spawn / attach / rehydrate, via a new `Agent.inherit()` that ingests the text
   with **fresh own-slot ids, RAM-only, and no durable re-record**. (Routing the
   replay through `ingestRaw`, which preserves source ids, would corrupt the
   target branch's `_seq` and re-graduate the entries on the next delete — hence a
   dedicated method.)
4. `/memory/search` recalls over a bridge-maintained **per-tenant base branch**
   (`tenantBase(tenant)`), rebuilt on restart and kept fresh as the tenant
   graduates agents.
5. The **global** agenticow base is now reserved for explicitly-curated shared
   infra (`addKnowledge`) — never fed by auto-graduation. Untagged/legacy agents
   keep the old global-base behavior.

At the storage layer (ADR-0008), `mem-sync` exports each tenant's memory to
`tenants/<tenant>/memory.json` (grouped from the durable log) — logical isolation
by subpath; the filespace stays owner-scoped.
title: ADR-0009: Per-tenant memory isolation via tenant-scoped graduation + replay

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** a tenant's vetted learnings reach only that tenant's future agents,
  never across tenants — closes risk #2; reuses the existing rehydrate/`ingestRaw`
  machinery and the single bridge (small blast radius on a *live* service); the
  shared-infra tier is still available, now opt-in; verified by a 22-check
  in-process suite + an HTTP round-trip on a scratch service + a live end-to-end
  test through the public backend, isolation surviving a restart.
- **Negative:** a tenant's `tbase` is **copied** into each of its agent branches at
  attach (duplication in RAM — fine at current corpus size, revisit at scale); the
  long-lived `/memory/search` tenant branch can lag a just-graduated entry until
  refreshed (handled on graduate + rebuilt on restart); pre-existing global-base
  content stays shared (isolation is not retroactive — we stop *new* leaks).
- **Neutral:** the tenant key shape comes straight from ADR-0003; hard storage
  isolation (per-tenant *filespace* + scoped token via the workspace gateway) is
  the documented multi-org upgrade and the next seam.

## Alternatives considered

- **Per-tenant hubs (separate `AgenticMemory` per tenant).** Conceptually cleanest
  and avoids per-branch duplication, but requires a tenant-aware bridge, N base
  files, and a rewrite of the delicate rehydrate/registry paths on a live service.
  Rejected for now on blast-radius grounds; the replay approach is reversible into
  this later if duplication or scale demands it.
- **Stop graduating entirely.** Rejected: graduation (a tenant's agents learning
  from each other) is a core feature; we scoped it, not removed it.
title: ADR-0009: Per-tenant memory isolation via tenant-scoped graduation + replay

text:
# ADR-0010: Per-tenant LucidLink filespace isolation (hard isolation)

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-30
- **Supersedes (storage layer of):** the subfolder note in [0009](0009-per-tenant-memory-isolation.md)
title: ADR-0010: Per-tenant LucidLink filespace isolation (hard isolation)

text:
## Context

ADR-0009 made graduation and recall tenant-scoped, and at the storage layer
(ADR-0008) `mem-sync` wrote each tenant's memory to `tenants/<tenant>/memory.json`
inside the **one shared `agenticow` filespace** — *logical* isolation by subpath.
Multi-org use wants **hard** isolation: a tenant's data physically separate, in its
own end-to-end-encrypted filespace, so a bug, a misrouted write, or a curious agent
cannot reach another tenant's bytes. ADR-0009 parked this as "per-tenant filespace +
scoped token via the workspace gateway."

We investigated whether that's buildable. Findings (all verified against the live
LucidLink Service API on spark `:3003` and the `lucidlink-mcp` 0.10 server on the Mac):

1. **Filespace lifecycle is fully API-automatable.** `POST/GET/DELETE
   /api/v1/filespaces` create/list/delete filespaces with LucidLink-managed storage
   (`storageOwner:lucidlink`). No portal step is required.
2. **Service-account tokens cannot be scoped to a filespace.** Per LucidLink, a
   service account "inherits the full permissions/scope of a workspace administrator."
   So the "scoped token per tenant" half of the ADR-0009 plan **is not available**;
   every token sees every filespace in the workspace.
3. **The forced command alone does not confine.** `LUCIDLINK_FILESPACE=<x>` only sets
   the *default* auto-link. `lucidlink-mcp` exposes `link_filespace` (annotated
   `stateful`, so **not** blocked by `READ_ONLY`, which only blocks additive/
   destructive ops) and has **no per-tool server-side exclude**. A holder of the
   bridge key can therefore `link_filespace` to any other filespace — verified
   directly. The previous "an agent cannot leave the namespace" guarantee held only
   for *harness agents* (via the spark-side `include` allowlist), **not** for a direct
   key holder such as `mem-sync`.

So the confinement boundary cannot be the token (can't scope it) or the forced-command
env (only a default) — it has to remove the filespace-switching tools from the wire.
title: ADR-0010: Per-tenant LucidLink filespace isolation (hard isolation)

text:
## Decision

**One dedicated LucidLink filespace per tenant (`stronghold-<tenant>`), with
confinement enforced by a stdio shim, not by token scope.**

1. **Provisioning** — `service/provision-tenant.sh <tenant>` (idempotent): creates the
   filespace via the Service API and polls to `ready`; generates a dedicated SSH key
   for the `stronghold` user (`id_ed25519_ll_<tenant>`); pins a forced command on the
   Mac's `authorized_keys`; and registers the tenant in
   `service/tenant-filespaces.json`.
2. **Confinement = `service/confine-mcp.py`** — the forced command runs this stdio
   JSON-RPC shim *instead of* `lucidlink-mcp` directly. The shim launches the real
   server (inheriting `LUCIDLINK_FILESPACE`) and **strips `link_filespace` /
   `list_filespaces`** from `tools/list` and rejects them on `tools/call`. With no way
   to switch or even enumerate other filespaces, the workspace-admin token is pinned to
   the single auto-linked filespace — for *any* caller of that key, harness or not.
3. **Routing** — `mem-sync.mjs` reads the registry: a registered tenant's export is
   written to `/stronghold-mem/memory.json` in its **own** filespace via its own key;
   an unregistered tenant falls back to the `agenticow` `tenants/<tenant>/` subfolder
   (ADR-0009 behaviour). The state key encodes the destination so a tenant promoted
   from subfolder → own filespace is re-pushed.
4. **Hardening the shared bridge** — the existing `agenticow` rw bridge forced command
   was switched to the same shim, closing the identical `link_filespace` hole there
   (it should only ever touch `agenticow`; the read-only bridge is intentionally left
   un-confined so it can browse multiple filespaces for document processing).

Verified end-to-end with reference tenant `pilot01`: `link_filespace(agenticow)` is
refused; `current_filespace` is `stronghold-pilot01`; `/stronghold-mem/base` does not
exist there (a clean, separate filespace); a real `mem-sync` run routes
`tbase:pilot01` into the pilot01 filespace while **excluding** the shared `base`
scope; and the `agenticow` namespace contains neither the secret nor a pilot01
subfolder.
title: ADR-0010: Per-tenant LucidLink filespace isolation (hard isolation)

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** hard *cryptographic* data separation per tenant — independent
  filespace, bucket, and encryption keyspace; confinement enforced **server-side at the
  bridge**, not just by a client allowlist, so even a direct key holder is pinned;
  provisioning is one idempotent script (no portal step); fully reversible
  (`DELETE /filespaces/{id}` + drop the key/line/registry entry).
- **Negative / residual:** the service-account **token is still workspace-admin** and
  lives on the Mac — a *Mac* compromise exposes every filespace regardless of the shim
  (the shim confines the spark-side key holders, not the token's own power). True
  token-level scoping awaits either LucidLink scoped-token support or a separate
  LucidLink **workspace** (hence its own token) per tenant — account/billing-level, not
  automatable from here. The shim is an extra moving part on the Mac. `mem-sync` opens
  the shared `agenticow` bridge even for a tenant-only sync (cheap, idempotent dir
  creation). One filespace per tenant grows LucidLink-managed storage/billing.
- **Neutral:** subfolder isolation (ADR-0009) remains the documented fallback for
  untenanted/legacy agents and for tenants not (yet) provisioned a filespace.

## Alternatives considered

- **Scoped service-account token per tenant** — the original ADR-0009 plan; not
  possible today (tokens are workspace-admin scope).
- **Per-tenant LucidLink *workspace* + its own token** — would give real token-level
  isolation, but creating workspaces is an account/billing operation outside the
  Service API used here; revisit if LucidLink exposes it or multi-org demands it.
- **Rely on the client-side `include` allowlist alone** — insufficient: it confines
  harness agents but not a direct holder of the bridge key (e.g. `mem-sync`, or a
  compromised `stronghold` process).
- **Subfolders in one shared filespace (ADR-0009)** — logical isolation only; kept as
  the fallback, not the multi-org answer.
title: ADR-0010: Per-tenant LucidLink filespace isolation (hard isolation)

text:
# ADR-0011: Token usage metering & observability across providers, calls, and tools

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-06-30

## Context

StrongHold routes work across local Ollama models, cloud Claude, OpenRouter, and
(ADR-0005) arbitrary OpenAI-compatible backends — a mix of *free/sovereign* local
spend and *paid* cloud spend. Every provider already returns token usage on each
call, but StrongHold **received and discarded it**. So there was no way to answer
the operational question the metaharness makes acute: *how many tokens did each
model / provider / tool actually burn?* Without that, the local-vs-cloud cost
tradeoff is invisible, and a runaway agentic loop or fanout shows up only on a
provider's bill, after the fact.

## Decision

Capture provider token usage at the router and surface it at three granularities:

1. **Normalize at the source.** Each model call's usage is read from the provider
   and normalized to `{ input, output, total }`. Ollama and OpenRouter read the
   OpenAI `usage` block; cloud Claude reads Anthropic `res.usage.{input_tokens,
   output_tokens}`. Compat backends (ADR-0005) report under provider label
   `compat:<name>`.
2. **Per call.** `chat`/`act`/`fanout` responses now include a `usage` block.
   `act` **sums** usage across every model call in the agentic loop; `fanout`
   **sums** across all sub-agents — so the number reflects the whole operation,
   not just the last hop.
3. **Cumulative (process).** The internal service `/healthz` reports
   `usageTotals = { totals, byProvider, byModel }`, each entry `{ input, output,
   total, calls }`, accumulated since process start — real-time per-model and
   per-backend attribution with no external dashboard.
4. **Per session (MCP).** The StrongHold MCP server keeps a per-session tally and
   exposes a new tool `stronghold_usage` (per-session totals + per-tool breakdown),
   computed client-side with no backend call. MCP tool count goes 11 → 12.
title: ADR-0011: Token usage metering & observability across providers, calls, and tools

text:
## Consequences

- **Positive:** real-time, per-model / per-provider / per-tool cost attribution
  with no external dashboard or telemetry pipeline; the free/sovereign-local vs
  paid-cloud spend is visible as you work; the public backend (:8771) needs no
  change — it proxies the new `usage` field verbatim. Verified live 2026-06-30:
  local qwen chat `{input:56,output:5,total:61}`, `deepseek-r1:32b {44,557,601}`,
  `/healthz.byModel` tracking each model by name, compat path reporting under
  `compat:<name>`.
- **Negative / known limitation:** the cumulative tally is currently
  **process-global, not per-tenant** — `usageTotals` aggregates across all callers,
  so it answers "what did this service burn?" not "what did tenant A burn?".
  Per-tenant cost attribution (keying totals by the ADR-0003 tenant) is the natural
  future refinement; the per-session MCP tally already gives a single client its own
  numbers.
- **Neutral:** numbers are token counts, not currency — price-per-model mapping
  (and any billing) is left to the consumer of `usageTotals` / `stronghold_usage`.

## Alternatives considered

- **External observability (OpenTelemetry / a metrics backend).** Rejected for now:
  another process and dependency for what is a small in-router tally; the data is
  most useful inline on the same call/`/healthz` surface callers already hit.
- **Keep discarding usage.** Rejected: the provider already hands it to us for free,
  and cost-blindness is untenable once routing spans free-local and paid-cloud.
title: ADR-0011: Token usage metering & observability across providers, calls, and tools

# StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

*StrongHold is our Harness as a Service (HaaS).*

For technical reviewers and security. Covers the full architecture, the trust
boundaries, every security and resilience control now in place, and the residual
risks (with honest mitigations) of the current `v0.1`.

StrongHold is a **sovereign, memory-centric AI-agent harness served as an API**,
running entirely on the owner's own hardware (two NVIDIA DGX Spark
supercomputers). Same capabilities as a cloud "AI agent service" — owned end to
end, data local. Repo: private GitHub `markt-heximal/StrongHold`; host root
`/home/markt/agenticow-ruflo-memory`.

Full feature reference: `docs/HARNESS.md`. Operations: `docs/OPS_RUNBOOK.md`.

---
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
## 1. Architecture

```
  Browser app (Lovable)  /  any client holding a per-user Bearer JWT
        │  HTTPS + Bearer JWT
        ▼
  Tailscale Funnel   https://spark-47d8.tail333a1d.ts.net/agentmem/v1   ── public internet edge
        │  funnel path /agentmem → 127.0.0.1:8771
        ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIER 2 — PUBLIC BACKEND   (Docker, node:http, :8771, Bearer JWT)    │
│  internet-facing edge · per-tenant isolation · stateless · no keys   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │  X-API-Key over host.docker.internal:8770   (NOT published via Funnel)
        ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIER 1 — INTERNAL SERVICE  (systemd, Fastify, :8770, X-API-Key)     │
│  memory + harness core · agent loop · sandbox · MCP hub · router     │
│   ├─ per-tenant COW vector memory (agenticow) + MiniLM-L6 (384-dim)  │
│   ├─ Docker code sandbox (ephemeral, --network none)                 │
│   ├─ MCP hub (stdio) → ruflo (local) , lucidlink (SSH-stdio bridge)  │
│   └─ model router → Ollama POOL | Anthropic | OpenRouter | OAI-compat│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │                                   │
        ▼ dual-GPU Ollama pool              ▼ SSH-stdio
  spark-47d8:11434  +  spark-a1d7:11434     ai-factory-mini (Mac) → uvx lucidlink-mcp
```

text:
### Two-tier design (defense in depth)

| Tier | File / port | Auth | Holds | Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier 2 — public backend** | `backend/server.js` · `:8771` | Bearer JWT | nothing sensitive — no model keys, no memory; per-tenant ownership map only | internet, via Funnel `/agentmem` |
| **Tier 1 — internal service** | `service/server.js` · `:8770` | `X-API-Key` | memory, model keys, code execution, MCP children | LAN/tailnet only; **never** published through the Funnel |

- The **public backend** is the only internet-facing component. It is a small,
  **zero-dependency** `node:http`+`node:crypto` process whose job is exactly:
  verify the JWT, derive the tenant, enforce per-tenant ownership, proxy to the
  internal service. It carries no model keys and no memory.
- The **internal service** holds everything sensitive. It authenticates callers
  with a shared `X-API-Key`. It binds all interfaces (so the backend and
  localhost can reach it on `:8770`) but the Tailscale Funnel path maps **only**
  to `:8771`, so the internal service is not internet-reachable.
- Backend → service hop is `host.docker.internal:8770`.

### Hosts

| Host | Role | Exposure |
|---|---|---|
| `spark-47d8` (DGX Spark, GB10) | Backend, internal service, sandbox, Funnel, one Ollama backend | `/agentmem` path public via Funnel |
| `spark-a1d7` (DGX Spark, GB10) | Second Ollama backend (`:11434`) in the pool | Cluster network only |
| `ai-factory-mini` (Apple Silicon Mac) | LucidLink MCP server, bridged to spark over SSH-stdio | Cluster network only |
| Anthropic / OpenRouter | Optional cloud models | Outbound, opt-in per request |
| Configured OpenAI-compatible backends (vLLM / llama.cpp / TGI / Open WebUI) | Optional, **config-driven** extra models | Outbound HTTP, opt-in per config |

text:
### Dual-GPU Ollama pool (`service/ollama.js`)

Both DGX Sparks run Ollama; local inference is a **load-balanced pool**, not a
single host. `OLLAMA_URLS` (csv) lists backends, default
`http://spark-a1d7:11434,http://localhost:11434`. Each backend gets a per-backend
slot (`OLLAMA_CONCURRENCY`, default `1` = one GPU, one job) → **true
parallelism** (2 GPUs = 2 concurrent inferences; verified: 2 concurrent requests
ran on both GPUs at once, wall-time ≈ single not 2×). A backend is healthy only
if reachable **AND** it has the model (a host still pulling auto-excludes itself).
On a call error the request **fails over to the sibling backend before the router
reaches cloud**. Background re-check `OLLAMA_HEALTH_MS` (`15000`). Legacy single
`OLLAMA_URL` is still honored.
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
### Model router (`service/router.js`)

One `tier` knob → ordered provider preference, failing over on error/timeout. The
caller never has to name a model.

| `tier` | Provider order |
|---|---|
| `fast` / `balanced` / `local` | `[local]` |
| `auto` (DEFAULT) | `[local → cloud → openrouter]` |
| `max` | `[cloud → openrouter → local]` |
| `openrouter` | `[openrouter → local]` |

- **local** = Ollama pool, model `qwen2.5-coder:32b`.
- **cloud** = Anthropic Claude `claude-opus-4-8` — only when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
  is set, otherwise those tiers resolve to local.
- **openrouter** = OpenAI-compatible (one key → GPT/Gemini/Llama/…), default slug
  `openai/gpt-4o`. An explicit `vendor/model` slug prefers OpenRouter but keeps
  local as failover.
- **compat** = a generic **OpenAI-compatible backend** provider
  (`service/openai-compat.js`) reaching ANY server that speaks
  `/v1/chat/completions` over HTTP — vLLM, llama.cpp `--server`, TGI, Open WebUI,
  LM Studio. A config registry of named backends `{ name, url, apiKey?, models? }`
  is **selectable purely by config, no code change** (source, first found: env
  `LLM_BACKENDS` inline JSON | `LLM_BACKENDS_CONFIG` path | `./llm-backends.json`).
  Target one with an explicit `<name>/<model>` slug (e.g. `webui/llama3.1:70b`);
  usage is metered under provider label `compat:<name>`.
- Routing is now **model-aware**: an explicit model slug *wins* — the router
  routes by what the model **is**, not the tier's default order. Bare model names
  still go to the Ollama pool (never shadowed); optional `tier → model` aliases
  (`TIER_MODELS` / `./tier-models.json`) let a bare `tier` resolve to a specific
  cluster model. Empty config = exactly the prior tier behavior (backward compatible).
- The response reports the `provider` + `model` that actually answered.
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
### Token / LLM usage metering (`service/router.js`, `service/mcp-stronghold.js`)

Every model call's token usage is now **captured** from the provider (previously
received upstream and discarded) and normalized to `{input, output, total}`
(Ollama / OpenRouter / compat read the OpenAI `usage` block; cloud Claude reads
`res.usage.{input_tokens,output_tokens}`). Three scopes:

- **Per call** — `chat` / `act` / `fanout` responses carry a `usage` block; `act`
  and `fanout` **sum** usage across every model call in the agentic loop / across
  all sub-agents.
- **Cumulative** — the internal service `/healthz` reports `usageTotals =
  { totals, byProvider, byModel }` (each `{input, output, total, calls}`) since
  process start. `healthz.router` also reports `compat` (backend names, or false)
  and `tierModels`.
- **Per session** — the StrongHold MCP server keeps a per-session tally exposed via
  a new 12th tool `stronghold_usage` (per-session totals + per-tool breakdown;
  client-side, no backend call). MCP tool count goes 11 → 12.

Net effect: **per-model and per-backend cost attribution with no external
dashboard** — local (free/sovereign) vs cloud (paid) spend is visible in real time.
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
### MCP external tools (`service/mcp-client.js`, `mcp-servers.json`)

Generic MCP stdio client + hub. Tools are namespaced `<server>__<tool>` and
auto-added to the act loop. Per-server `include`/`exclude` allowlist.

- **ruflo** — `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest mcp start`; 305 tools curated down to 8
  (`memory_search`/`store`/`retrieve`, `swarm_status`, `agent_list`,
  `task_create`/`status`, `system_status`).
- **lucidlink** — read-only access to LucidLink filespaces. The package
  `lucidlink-mcp` runs on **ai-factory-mini** (spark is aarch64 and the package
  has no ARM-Linux wheel), bridged to spark via **SSH-stdio**
  (`command: ssh … uvx lucidlink-mcp`). Read-only + core toolset = **9 tools**:
  `list_filespaces`, `link_filespace`, `current_filespace`, `whoami`, `read_file`,
  `list_files`, `find_files`, `grep_files`, `read_lines`. The `sa_live:` token
  lives in `~/.lucidlink/mcp-config.json` **on the Mac**, never in git.
- **lucidlink-rw** — read **and** write, confined to the `agenticow` filespace =
  the StrongHold common memory namespace (`/stronghold-mem`). The Mac
  `authorized_keys` forced command pins `LUCIDLINK_FILESPACE=agenticow` **and runs
  the `confine-mcp.py` shim** (ADR-0010), which strips `link_filespace`/
  `list_filespaces` so the key cannot switch to or enumerate any other filespace —
  the include allowlist also drops destructive ops. (The read-only `lucidlink`
  bridge is intentionally *not* shimmed: it browses many filespaces for document
  processing.)

  **Per-tenant isolation of memory storage (ADR-0010, 2026-06-30):** each provisioned
  tenant gets its **own** end-to-end-encrypted LucidLink filespace
  (`stronghold-<tenant>`, separate bucket + keyspace), created by
  `service/provision-tenant.sh` and reached via a dedicated key whose forced command
  runs the same shim pinned to that filespace. `mem-sync` routes a registered tenant's
  export into its own filespace (`tenant-filespaces.json`); an unregistered tenant
  falls back to the `agenticow` `tenants/<tenant>/` subfolder (ADR-0009 logical
  isolation). **Residual:** LucidLink service-account tokens are workspace-admin scope
  (cannot be narrowed per filespace), so the confinement boundary is the shim, not the
  token — a *Mac* compromise (where the token lives) still exposes all filespaces. Full
  token-level isolation awaits LucidLink scoped-token support or a per-tenant workspace.

text:
## 2. Trust boundaries

```
  ── boundary A ──   public internet ⇄ Tailscale Funnel ⇄ backend :8771
        only authentication: a valid Bearer JWT. /health is the only unauth route.

  ── boundary B ──   backend :8771 ⇄ internal service :8770
        only authentication: shared X-API-Key. Not reachable from the internet.

  ── boundary C ──   internal service ⇄ MCP child processes (ruflo, lucidlink)
        children get a MINIMAL env (no service secrets); lucidlink also crosses
        an SSH-stdio hop to a different host (ai-factory-mini).

  ── boundary D ──   internal service ⇄ sandbox container (rootless Docker)
        --network none, cap-drop ALL, read-only, non-root; no host FS, no egress.
        Daemon is rootless under the unprivileged `stronghold` user → container
        UID 0 maps to a subuid, so even a container escape gets no host root.

  ── boundary E ──   internal service ⇄ cloud / configured model backends (opt-in, outbound)
        only on tier:auto-fallback / max / openrouter, or an explicit compat
        slug; local tiers never leave. Compat backends speak only OpenAI
        /v1/chat/completions; their keys + URLs live solely in gitignored
        llm-backends.json (not in the repo).
```

| # | Boundary | Crossed by | Control |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Internet ↔ backend | Bearer JWT only | JWT verification + per-tenant isolation; TLS via Funnel |
| B | Backend ↔ internal service | `X-API-Key` | shared key; service not on the Funnel |
| C | Service ↔ MCP children | minimal env allowlist | no secrets leak to third-party MCP processes |
| D | Service ↔ sandbox | hardened container flags + rootless daemon | network/cap/FS isolation; escape maps to an unprivileged subuid, not host root |
| E | Service ↔ cloud / configured LLM backends | per-request / per-config opt-in | local-by-default; egress only on chosen tiers or an explicit compat slug; compat keys + URLs only in gitignored `llm-backends.json` |

text:
## 3. Authentication & multi-tenancy (`backend/server.js`)

Public auth is **Bearer JWT, algorithm auto-detected from the token header**.

### Asymmetric Supabase (RS/ES/PS)

Verified against the JWKS of the token's **own issuer**
(`https://<ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1`), so **any** of the owner's Supabase
projects work with zero config. Tenant key = `"<ref>:<sub>"`. The same user UUID
in two different projects is two isolated tenants.

- **Project allowlist** — `SUPABASE_ALLOWED_REFS` (csv). **Fail closed**: with no
  allowlist set, asymmetric tokens are **rejected** unless `SUPABASE_ALLOW_ANY=1`
  is explicitly set. Issuer shape is constrained by `SUPABASE_ISS_REGEX`.
- **JWKS serve-last-good** — if the IdP is briefly unreachable, the stale cached
  key is used rather than rejecting every login. (Resilience without failing open
  on identity, since the cached key is the IdP's own published key.)

### HS256

Verified against `JWT_SECRET`; tenant `"hs:<sub>"`. Intended for the prototype /
single-secret case.

### Isolation

`userId` is the `sub` claim, **never** taken from the request body. Per-tenant
agent ownership is enforced — a caller can only see/use/delete agents they own;
cross-tenant access returns **404**. Verified: user B cannot reach user A's agent.
`GET /health` is the only unauthenticated route.

---

## 4. Security controls (current)

All four hardening tranches are DONE and verified live (2026-06-29).

### Fail-closed secrets (refuse-to-boot)

Both tiers refuse to start on a default / weak / missing key:

- Internal service: `API_KEY` is **required, no default**.
- Backend: `JWT_SECRET` and `INTERNAL_API_KEY` must be **≥ 24 chars**; shorter →
  refuse to boot.
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
### Rate limiting & concurrency caps

| Control | Env / default | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Per-tenant token bucket | `RATE_BURST` `30` capacity, refill `RATE_PER_SEC` `1`/s | heavy ops (`act`/`fanout`/`chat`/`sandbox`) cost `HEAVY_COST` `5` → **429 + Retry-After** |
| Global heavy-op concurrency | `MAX_INFLIGHT_HEAVY` `4` | 5th simultaneous heavy job across all tenants → **429** |
| Global sandbox container cap | `SANDBOX_MAX_CONCURRENCY` `4` | sandbox runs queue beyond 4 |
| Request body limit | `MAX_BODY_BYTES` `1000000` | oversize → **413**; malformed JSON → **400** |
| Per-request loop budget | `ACT_BUDGET_MS` `180000` wall-clock + `MAX_TOOLCALLS_PER_STEP` `8` | bounds a runaway agent loop |

### Sandbox isolation (`/sandbox/run`, `run_code` tool)

Each run is an ephemeral Docker container: `--network none`, `--cap-drop ALL`,
`--read-only` rootfs, **non-root**, `/tmp` tmpfs **noexec**, and memory / CPU /
pids / wall-clock limited, `--rm` on exit. Languages: python, node, bash. Public
RCE-by-design is gated behind the JWT **and** the rate limit, the global heavy-op
cap, and the global sandbox cap above. `SANDBOX_ENABLED` is a kill switch.

The sandbox runs on a **rootless Docker daemon** owned by the dedicated
unprivileged `stronghold` service user (not the rootful host daemon). This is a
defence-in-depth layer *under* the container flags: even a full container escape
lands as one of `stronghold`'s subuids (container UID 0 → host subuid 165536+),
with no privilege over host files or the rootful socket. The harness process
itself cannot reach `/var/run/docker.sock`.

### Minimal MCP child env

MCP children receive only a safe env allowlist (PATH/HOME/…) plus the per-server
`env` override — **never** the service secrets. Verified: the ruflo child env has
no `ANTHROPIC` / `OPENROUTER` / `INTERNAL` / `JWT` / `LUCIDLINK` keys. Third-party
MCP processes therefore cannot exfiltrate model keys or the internal API key.
title: StrongHold — Architecture & Security Brief

text:
### MCP resilience

A dead MCP child (SSH bridge drop, ruflo crash) is detected and
**auto-respawned with exponential backoff** (1s → 30s cap). `has()`/`call()` are
gated on `ready`, tools are read live so respawns restore them, and MCP boot is
**parallel** (servers start concurrently). `/healthz` shows per-server
`ready`/`restarts`/`lastExit` and goes `degraded` when a server is down.

### Timeouts & failover

Every model call has a timeout so a hung host triggers failover, not a hang:
`OLLAMA_TIMEOUT_MS` / `OPENROUTER_TIMEOUT_MS` / `CLOUD_TIMEOUT_MS` default
`120000`; backend→internal non-stream `INTERNAL_TIMEOUT_MS` `300000`. A GPU
semaphore makes fan-out queue instead of dogpiling a single GPU.

### Durability (no "stored" lies)

The append-only durable log is the source of truth. `remember` **flushes to disk
BEFORE acknowledging** the write (no false "stored" 200s). A corrupt durable /
owners file is backed up to `.corrupt.<ts>` and the service **refuses to start**
rather than silently wiping it. The backend flushes `owners.json` on
SIGTERM/SIGINT. Restart policy: internal `Restart=on-failure`; backend Docker
`restart=unless-stopped`.

### Health info-leak closed

Unauthenticated `/healthz` returns only `{status, uptime}`; the detailed
diagnostics (base vectors, agent counts, MCP/Ollama internals, etc.) require the
API key. The public backend's `GET /health` returns only `{status, baseVectors,
internal}` and is intentionally the one unauthenticated route.

### Secrets handling

Secrets live **only** on the host — `/etc/agentmem-internal.env` and
`backend/.env` — never in git, never baked into the Docker image. Model keys live
only in the internal service. The LucidLink `sa_live:` token lives only on
ai-factory-mini. The OpenAI-compatible backends' API keys and private URLs live
**only** in the gitignored `llm-backends.json` (and `tier-models.json`) on the
host — only the `*.example` templates are committed; the internal service speaks
nothing but OpenAI `/v1/chat/completions` to those backends.

| Request | Leaves the box? | To |
|---|---|---|
| memory ops, recall, embeddings | No | local MiniLM-L6 (384-dim) |
| `/sandbox/run`, `run_code` | No | local Docker |
| `tier:fast` / `balanced` / `local` chat/act | No | Ollama pool on the cluster |

## 5. Residual risks (v0.1) — honest mitigations

| # | Risk | Severity | Status / mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Harness runs as a docker-group user.** An RCE in the harness process *itself* (not the sandbox — the host service) would have Docker socket access, i.e. effectively **host-root**. | ~~High if reached~~ | **MITIGATED 2026-06-29.** The internal service now runs as a dedicated unprivileged user `stronghold` (uid 1001, **not** in the docker group) wired to its **own rootless Docker daemon** (`unix:///run/user/1001/docker.sock`). The harness process is denied the rootful socket, and container UID 0 maps to `stronghold`'s subuid range — powerless on the host. | 2 | **Graduation used to promote to a single cross-tenant base.** Deleting / graduating an agent promoted its vetted learnings into one shared base, so graduated content became visible across tenants via `/memory/search`. | ~~Medium~~ | **MITIGATED 2026-06-30.** Graduation is now **per-tenant**: each agent is tagged with its tenant (JWT-derived) on spawn, and `terminateAndGraduate` re-scopes its learnings into a per-tenant durable scope `tbase:<tenant>` — **never** the global base. A tenant's future agents inherit only `tbase:<tenant>`, and `/memory/search` recalls over a per-tenant base branch, so no tenant reads another's graduated content. | 4 | **Allowlist breadth + cloud spend.** Any user from any allowlisted Supabase project authenticates, and cloud / compat tiers cost money per call. | Medium (cost/abuse) | Per-tenant token bucket + global heavy-op cap now bound abuse rate; keep `SUPABASE_ALLOWED_REFS` tight and avoid `SUPABASE_ALLOW_ANY=1` in production. **Spend is now observable**: token-usage metering (§Token / LLM usage metering) attributes tokens per model / provider (`byProvider` / `byModel` on `/healthz`), pairing with the rate limits / heavy-op caps to make spend visible per backend. **Refinement:** the metering tally is process-global today (not yet per-tenant), and hard spend caps remain a follow-up. |

| 6 | **Credential hygiene.** Keys were entered operationally and live in host env files. | Low | Keys are root-only in host env files and not internet-exposed; rotate at the owner's discretion. Consider a secrets manager if the fleet grows. |

# StrongHold — Developer Quickstart

*StrongHold is our Harness as a Service (HaaS).*

A per-user memory + agent API you can call from any app. Local-first models with optional cloud
escalation; you never name a model unless you want to. Every response reports the `provider` and
`model` that actually answered.

- **Base URL:** `https://spark-47d8.tail333a1d.ts.net/agentmem/v1`

## 4. Agents (CRUD)

```bash
# create — agentType is any string; label is optional
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{"agentType":"assistant","label":"support-bot"}' $BASE/agents
# list yours
curl -s -H "$AUTH" $BASE/agents
# get one
curl -s -H "$AUTH" $BASE/agents/$AID
# delete — GRADUATES vetted memories into your shared base (see §10)
curl -s -X DELETE -H "$AUTH" $BASE/agents/$AID
```

Agents are owned by your tenant; another tenant's agentId resolves to `404`.

## 5. Memories — `remember` & `recall`

```bash
# remember — store text on an agent's private memory.
# Durable: the call doesn't return 2xx until it's flushed to disk (no "stored" lies).
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{"text":"Customer prefers email over phone."}' \
  $BASE/agents/$AID/memories

# recall — semantic search of THIS agent's memory (+ your base), k results
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{"query":"how to contact the customer","k":5}' \
  $BASE/agents/$AID/recall
```

`/memory/search` is the same idea but searches only **your tenant's base** (your graduated
memories — never another tenant's), not a specific agent:

```bash
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{"query":"launch date","k":5}' $BASE/memory/search
```

## 6. `act` — the agentic loop (with tier + tools)

`/act` runs a recall → think → call tools → feed results back → answer loop. It can **write & run
code** in the secure sandbox (`python`/`node`/`bash`, no network), call memory tools (`recall_memory`,
`remember`), and use connected external MCP tools. The response carries a `steps[]` trace of every
tool call plus the `provider`/`model` that answered.

```bash
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{
  "prompt": "Compute the 20th Fibonacci number and remember it.",
  "tier": "auto",
  "profile": "code",
  "maxSteps": 6
}' $BASE/agents/$AID/act
```

Knobs:
- `tier` — model routing, see §9.
- `profile` / `tools` — per-task tool selection, see §8.
- `maxSteps` — cap on tool-using iterations.
- `recallK` — how many memories to inject up front.

## 7. `fanout` — parallel sub-agents

Up to **8** ephemeral workers run tasks in parallel, results aggregated, then dismissed (fan-out
workers do **not** graduate memory). `tier` / `profile` / `tools` set defaults for the batch; each
task can also be an object that overrides `prompt`, `tools`, and `profile` per task.

```bash
curl -s -H "$AUTH" -H "$CT" -d '{
  "tier": "auto",
  "profile": "research",
  "tasks": [
    "Summarize our Q3 launch plan.",
    { "prompt": "List the open files for the redesign.", "profile": "files" },
    { "prompt": "Sanity-check this regex in code.", "tools": ["run_code"] }
  ],
  "agentType": "worker",
  "maxStepsPer": 4
}' $BASE/agents/$AID/fanout
```

text:
## 8. Per-task tool selection (`profile` / `tools`)

By default a task may use **all** tools (back-compat). To scope it, pass either a named `profile`
or an explicit `tools` allowlist. Selection is enforced in two layers: it filters the tools
*offered* to the model AND blocks them at dispatch — a call to a non-permitted tool returns
"not permitted".

**`tools` allowlist syntax** — an array of: bare built-in names (e.g. `"run_code"`,
`"recall_memory"`, `"remember"`), namespaced MCP tools `"<server>__<tool>"` (e.g.
`"lucidlink__grep_files"`), or `"*"` wildcard.

**Built-in `profile` names** (defined in `tool-profiles.json`, merged over defaults):

| `profile` | What it allows |
|---|---|
| `all` | every tool (same as omitting) |
| `memory` | memory tools only (recall / remember) |
| `code` | the code sandbox |
| `files` | LucidLink filespace tools (`lucidlink__*`) |
| `research` | research-oriented bundle |
| `lucid-readonly` | read-only LucidLink access |

Discover what's wired up: **`GET /tools`** returns `builtin`, `mcp` (per-server), `available`
(all tool names you can put in `tools`), and `profiles`.

> **LucidLink filespace tools** let an agent read & search your team's LucidLink files
> (`list_filespaces`, `read_file`, `list_files`, `find_files`, `grep_files`, `read_lines`, …),
> exposed as `lucidlink__*` and read-only. Use `profile: "files"` or `"lucid-readonly"` to enable them.
title: StrongHold — Developer Quickstart

text:
## 9. The `tier` knob (model routing)

Optional on `chat` / `act` / `fanout`. One knob picks an ordered provider preference; the router
fails over on error/timeout. You never have to name a model.

| `tier` | Provider order | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `fast` / `balanced` / `local` | local | on-prem Ollama (`qwen2.5-coder:32b`) — free, private |
| *(omitted)* / `auto` | local → cloud → openrouter | **default**: local first, escalate if needed |
| `max` | cloud → openrouter → local | best reasoning (Claude), cloud-first |
| `openrouter` | openrouter → local | OpenRouter (GPT/Gemini/Llama/…), local fallback |

`local` is load-balanced across both DGX Spark GPUs. `cloud` (Claude `claude-opus-4-8`) is only
available when the host has an Anthropic key configured; otherwise those tiers resolve to local.

Power user: pass an explicit `vendor/model` slug as `model` (e.g.
`{ "model": "google/gemini-2.0-flash" }`) to target a specific OpenRouter model (keeps local as
failover). The response always reports the actual `provider` + `model`.

tokens, send `Accept: text/event-stream` and read the SSE stream — but you **cannot** use the

## 13. Gotchas

- **Streaming:** use `fetch` + a stream reader with `Accept: text/event-stream`, **not**
  `EventSource` (no auth header). Streaming is local-model only. See §10.
- **Your tenant base:** deleting an agent *graduates* its memories into **your tenant's** base
  (scope `tbase:<tenant>`), which `/memory/search` reads and your future agents inherit. Raw
  private memories stay per-agent; graduated ones are shared **only within your tenant** — never
  with other tenants. (A separate global base holds explicitly-curated cross-tenant infra only.)
- **Latency:** the local 32B model takes ~20–30 s per step; `tier:"max"`/`openrouter` (cloud)
  are faster. Multi-step `/act` and `fanout` are correspondingly slower on local.
- **Rate limits:** heavy ops (act/fanout/chat/sandbox) cost more from your token bucket; expect
  `429` + `Retry-After` under burst, and `413` on bodies over ~1 MB.

## 14. Use StrongHold from Claude Code (MCP)

StrongHold ships a **stdio MCP server** (`service/mcp-stronghold.js`, zero-dependency)
that exposes the public API as native tools to Claude Code or any MCP client. It is the
mirror image of §12 in `HARNESS.md`: there StrongHold is an MCP *client* (it consumes
LucidLink/ruflo); here StrongHold is an MCP *server*.

**One-time setup** (on the host, or any box that can reach the backend):

```bash

#    Reads JWT_SECRET from backend/.env at runtime — never prints it.
node service/mint-stronghold-token.mjs --url http://localhost:8771 --agent-type researcher
# (off-box: --url https://spark-47d8.tail333a1d.ts.net/agentmem/v1)

# 2. Register the server with Claude Code (user scope = all projects).
claude mcp add stronghold --scope user -- node /ABS/PATH/service/mcp-stronghold.js

# 3. Confirm.
claude mcp list            # -> stronghold ... ✔ Connected
```

> New MCP servers become callable (`mcp__stronghold__*`) **after a session reload/restart**.

**Tools** (12): `stronghold_health`, `stronghold_list_agents`, `stronghold_spawn_agent`,
`stronghold_delete_agent`, `stronghold_remember`, `stronghold_recall`,
`stronghold_memory_search`, `stronghold_chat`, `stronghold_act`, `stronghold_fanout`,
`stronghold_run_code`, `stronghold_usage` (per-session token totals + per-tool breakdown,
client-side — see §15). The memory/chat/act tools take an **optional** `agentId`; omit it
and the server lazily spawns one default agent and caches its id (zero-config).

**Config** (`~/.stronghold/mcp.json`, or override per key with env vars):

| Key | Env override | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `url` | `STRONGHOLD_URL` | Public backend base (default `http://localhost:8771`) |
| `token` | `STRONGHOLD_JWT` | Bearer JWT (per-tenant) |
| `agent` | `STRONGHOLD_AGENT` | Default agentId (auto-cached on first use) |
| `defaultAgentType` | `STRONGHOLD_DEFAULT_AGENT_TYPE` | Type for the lazily-spawned agent |
| — | `STRONGHOLD_CONFIG` | Alternate config-file path |

The minted token uses the **HS256 prototype tenant** (`hs:<sub>`) — it bypasses the
Supabase allowlist and is invalidated if `JWT_SECRET` is rotated. Remove the server with
